title: Joseph Interprets Pharaoh's Dreams
summary: Pharaoh's paired dreams trouble his court, but Joseph says their interpretation belongs to God. He explains that seven years of abundance will be followed by seven years of famine, then proposes storing grain during the good years. Pharaoh appoints Joseph to carry out that plan. The episode turns a prisoner's ability to interpret dreams into authority over Egypt's food supply, and later Joseph understands this rise as part of how many lives—including his family's—were preserved.
historical_context: Genesis places the episode in Pharaoh's court and shows Joseph moving from interpreting the dreams to proposing and administering a famine-preparation plan. The narrative's focus is on royal decision-making and grain storage as the response to predicted scarcity. These are details in the story; the sources listed here do not independently identify Pharaoh, date the episode, or document Joseph's office.
canonical_context: Joseph's rise explains how Israel enters Egypt, setting the stage for both preservation and later oppression.
literary_context: The two dreams repeat the same pattern, and Joseph explicitly says their repetition means the matter is firmly decided. His interpretation is followed by practical advice, so the scene moves from revelation to policy and then to Joseph's elevation. That reversal matters in Joseph's larger story: the person who had been imprisoned now oversees the plan that will sustain people during famine. Later, Joseph's own words about preservation make clear that the outcome does not erase the harm he suffered.
covenantal_significance: Genesis 45:4–8 and 50:20 look back on the famine and Joseph's rise as means by which many lives were preserved. Joseph includes his family in that survival, but the text does not say that the harm done to him was good in itself. The story connects divine purpose with human actions and their consequences, holding together preservation and the reality of the earlier wrongs.
canonical_role: Connects patriarchal promise to the Egypt setting from which the exodus story will emerge.

related_objects.notes: Egypt later becomes the place of bondage and deliverance

scripture_references.notes: God works through evil for preservation

interpretive_notes.note: Genesis presents Joseph's wisdom as divine gift, not merely court technique or political skill.
